name: m2_extract_module_refactor
stressor: extract/move module + rewire ALL importers: the moved symbols, their 5 importers, and the public re-export must all repoint consistently while a same-named distractor stays untouched
source_note: Grounded in the Move Function / Move Module refactoring (Martin Fowler, Refactoring 2nd ed., catalog 'Move Function' aka Move Method, https://refactoring.com/catalog/moveFunction.html) and the empirically-observed 'Move Class' refactoring category that RefactoringMiner detects in real commit histories (Tsantalis et al., RefactoringMiner; https://github.com/tsantalis/RefactoringMiner). The defining mechanic of these refactorings is that after relocating a symbol you MUST update every reference/importer to its new home, leaving no dangling old reference. The same-name distractor mirrors RefactoringMiner's documented Move-Method/Move-Class false-positive confusion: a symbol with an identical name in another module that must NOT be repointed. Purpose-built 'taskq' package (9 modules) authored for this benchmark; pure stdlib, self-contained.
discriminator: The correct fix touches 6 interdependent files in lockstep: create taskq/retry.py with the two moved symbols, then rewire taskq/__init__.py (public re-export), worker.py, dispatcher.py, queue.py (qualified core.RetryPolicy + direct import), and runner.py to import from taskq.retry -- with the old taskq/core.py definitions removed so no dangling '.core import RetryPolicy/compute_backoff' survives. Two files are traps: scheduler.py defines its OWN unrelated RetryPolicy (and legitimately imports Job from core, which stays), and telemetry.py mentions both names only as string labels; both must stay byte-identical. A bounded-slice agent holds the whole import graph in its working set and repoints every site consistently; a growing-transcript agent must re-derive the importer list repeatedly and tends to either miss one importer (leaving a dangling core import), leave the symbols duplicated in core.py, or over-apply a blanket replace that corrupts scheduler.py's same-named local class.
